coverage.assessment: The pre-1400 evidence (instruments, architect's sequence) was cut, so 'a sequence' and the Middle Ages claim dangle. The salt image that motivates 'jump' was also removed.
Cutting 'Man could no longer hold it off' leaves 'his wrists' with no antecedent; the nearest male name is Mill. Other referents (the new American in 1964, 'the boy') hold.
No dialogue. The two retained textbook quotations are framed and attributed correctly.

The figures 30,000, 234 and 300 million are intact, and 'for convenience' survives for the squares formula. However, 'Any other formula would do as well', the temporary intensity assumption, and the grounds for extending the ratio to 1600 were cut.
The historian's limited, borrowed knowledge of science remains visible ('perplexed but laborious follower', 'waited only to be taught'). There is no premature disclosure.

The Paris gentleman and the 'sort of God' passage survive. The self-deprecating 'never able to acquire knowledge' and 'failed to educate even the generation of 1870' are gone, as is the cadenced 'groaned and shrieked and shuddered'.
The 'mental inertia of science' and man's inability to stop were cut, weakening the inertia/tragedy thread. The unity-to-multiplicity close holds.
Dependencies 0 and 1 are intact at both endpoints. The Terebratula joke (dependency 2) was dropped, although partner 017 still sets it up.

strengths: All eight verbatim passages survive intact, including the comet line that chapter 037's 'pass perihelion' picks up.
The steamer figures (30,000 and 234) and the 300 million tons of coal are exact, with no invented numbers.
The revision restores the source's 'to suffer dissipation altogether', correcting the first draft's 'or suffer'.
The timid Paris gentleman and the bombs doubling every ten years keep their comic deflation of the cosmic register.
The new American as 'a sort of God' who may sit with Gibbon in 1964 is preserved in full cadence.
summary: The revision keeps every verbatim anchor, all planned figures, the comet, coal and squares frame, the Paris gentleman, the 1964 Gibbon return, and the closing jump. Two cuts made in this pass leave visible breaks. 'Forces grasped his wrists' now has no antecedent, and 'a sequence is manifestly there' has lost the medieval evidence it summarized. Other cuts thin the hedges and authorities behind the extrapolation, remove Adams's self-deprecation as a failed teacher, drop the inertia-of-science irony and the salt phase-change image that prepares 'jump', and cut the optional Terebratula joke. Most of these losses originate in the revision; the first draft preserved them.
